provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation: Generator mechanism: there is a 9x9 background (6) and two solid 3x3 blocks in opposite corners. Each block's colour also has scattered stray cells. In the output the strays vanish, and each stray is re-attached to its own block's face. A stray beyond the block's column span (with at most one row of overhang) is moved to the column adjacent to that face. Its row is clamped into the block's row span. Strays beyond the row span are handled symmetrically. Because of the generator's 'shift' step, a stray can sit one row or column outside the face span. The generator then clamps it back into the span; it is not a diagonal slide. Example: (3,5) maps to (2,3) for the top-left block. The emitted program states this geometrically in visible coordinates. Background is palette[6], with a most-common-colour fallback. Each other colour's block is its largest 4-connected component. For each stray, it takes the per-axis distance outside the block's bounding box. Attachment uses the face along the axis with the larger distance, with the other coordinate clamped into the block span. All strays are erased first, then all targets are painted. The definition uses only bounding boxes, faces and clamping, so it is D4-equivariant. It needs no axis specialization, and colour roles come from the pixels. I hand-checked it against both train pairs and the test pair.
draft_notes.limitations: 1) Archived solver and rule text diverge from the constructor. They slide strays diagonally until they hit a same-colour cell. For shifted strays farther than 2 along the main axis, the generator instead clamps the cross coordinate. Example: (3,5) for the top-left block maps to (2,3) in the generator, but the archived solver gives (1,3). The archived program will therefore fail some fresh pairs. This factory follows the constructor, which agrees with all fixtures. Host review recommended. 2) In the generator domain, the main-axis distance always exceeds the cross-axis distance (>=2 vs <=1), and targets never collide, so no stacking occurs. Equal nonzero offsets cannot be generated. The program sends them to the diagonal corner cell, an arbitrary out-of-domain choice. Colliding targets simply overwrite each other. 3) The generator's 'sometimes shift' comment reflects random latent choices. The resulting positions are visible, so no hidden tie-break affects the answer. 4) The program assumes one dominant block per colour, the largest component. Strays of a colour that has no block are not meaningful. 5) Demonstrations are not used.

independent_source_review.mechanism: The scene is a 9x9 grid with background palette[6] and two solid 3x3 blocks in opposite corners. Each block's colour also has stray cells. In the output every stray is removed and re-attached to its own block. It goes to the cell just outside the face on the axis where it lies farther outside the block. Its other coordinate is clamped into the block's span. The constructor applies this as r>3→(3,min(c,2)) and c>3→(min(r,2),3) for pair[0], and as r<5→(5,max(c,6)) and c<5→(max(r,6),5) for pair[1]. The factory finds each colour's block as its largest component (size first, then rectangularity). It takes per-axis distances outside the block's bounding box, picks the face on the axis with the larger distance, and clamps the cross coordinate. It erases all strays and only then paints all targets.
evidence: Constructor domain, pair[0]. Top strays have rows 0-2 (a row-2 stray may shift to 3) and cols 4-8, so ox=c-2>=2 and oy<=1. Left strays have rows 4-8 and cols 0-2 (a col-2 stray may shift to 3), so oy>=2 and ox<=1. Pair[1] is symmetric. The main-axis distance therefore always strictly exceeds the cross-axis distance, so face selection is never tied.

Factory target expressions match the constructor exactly. For oy>ox: ty=y1+1 or y0-1 and tx=clamp(x). For ox>oy: tx=x1+1 or x0-1 and ty=clamp(y). Example: (3,5) for the top-left block gives (2,3) in both.

No stray component can reach block size. Top strays have distinct sampled rows and the shift only maps 2→3. A stray is never 4-adjacent to its own block, and top and left strays of the same colour are never 4-adjacent; the same holds for pair[1]. Every stray component has at most 3 cells against the block's 9, so the largest-component choice always picks the true block.

Targets cannot collide. Rows and cols are sampled distinctly, and the shift maps 2→3 (or 6→5) onto targets that remain distinct. The colour-0 targets (col 3 rows 0-2, row 3 cols 0-2) are disjoint from the colour-1 targets (row 5 cols 6-8, col 5 rows 6-8). The draw() rejection prevents strays from overlapping blocks or each other. Erasing everything before painting means a later colour's erasure cannot remove an earlier colour's placement.

Hand-checked all fixtures. Train 1: colour 9 lands at (0,3),(2,3),(3,0..2); colour 4 lands at (5,6..8),(7,5),(8,5). Train 2: (3,4)→(2,3), (5,4)→(6,5), (4,1)→(3,1), (8,2)→(3,2), plus the column 3 and column 5 targets. Test: (5,1)→(3,1), row 3 of colour 8→row 5, (5,4)→(6,5), (7,1)→(7,5), (8,3)→(8,5). All match the approved outputs.
The solver works directly on the visible grid using bounding boxes, faces and clamping. It has no whole-grid untransform/retransform wrapper and is D4-equivariant without any axis constants.
The random 'shift' latent only changes visible input positions; the label depends only on those visible positions. No hidden tie-break reaches the answer.
f28a3cbb is not in the require_colour_evidence task list, so the function returns early. The task involves no arbitrary colour association; colour roles come from the visible pixels.
nonblocking_limits: The archived program and rule text use a diagonal slide that stops at a same-colour cell. This diverges from the constructor whenever a stray is offset by one on the cross axis and by at least 3 on the main axis. Example: (3,6) gives (0,3) in the archive but (2,3) in the constructor. The demonstrations and test only contain cross offset 1 with main offset 2, where the two rules agree, so the visible episode does not disambiguate them. The factory follows the constructor. The constructor's clamp rule is a coherent rule (the nearest face-adjacent cell), not an indexing bug.
Equal nonzero offsets send a stray to the diagonal corner cell, and colliding targets simply overwrite each other. Both cases are out of domain because the constructor cannot produce them.
The solver assumes each non-background colour has one dominant block. Colours without a block are undefined.
Demonstrations are not used, which is acceptable for this deterministic geometric rule.

draft_notes.host_review: Host read full constructor, direct program and archived transform. Constructor clamps off-span strays to nearest block face; archived transform slides with constant diagonal direction and can run to an edge or earlier same-colour placement. Both fit canonical pairs but disagree on e.g(3,6) near top-left block. Generator labels unchanged. New same-query rule gate compares clamp against archived-style slides with all eight spatial tie orders; rejects episodes lacking a distinguishing demonstration if query predictions differ. For generated inputs block size9 uniquely dominates stray components atmost3; primary displacement>=2, cross displacement<=1, so face choice is strict. Sampled row/column uniqueness prevents target collisions. Hash-matched1000/8000/16 audit and1000uniqueinputs already passed.
